faq.q: What is an AI video for YouTube Shorts ads?
faq.a: A tall product video made from your photo or your product link, with an [AI actor](/ai-video-generation/ai-actors) and a voice you can edit. It is not a real customer review.

faq.q: Can I customize the script, actor, and visuals?
faq.a: Yes. Rewrite the script, swap the actor, change the voice, and adjust the scene before you download.

faq.q: What does a Short cost in credits?
faq.a: A video costs 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. Credits are what your monthly plan gives you to spend. You see the cost before you start. If a file fails, those credits come back on their own. There is no free plan.

faq.q: Are AI videos allowed in YouTube ads?
faq.a: Follow Google's current rules for checking ads, and for saying when a video is made by AI, on the day you publish. We do not send the ad in for you, and we do not promise it will be approved. Do not present a generated actor as a real customer.

faq.q: How should I treat the actors and voices?
faq.a: They are AI presenters, not people you hired. You can change the tone and the language. Do not say a shopper will think they are a real customer.

faq.q: Does a Short start from a product link?
faq.a: Yes. Paste a product page link, or upload a photo. A wide 16:9 ad, the kind that plays in the YouTube player, is a separate file. Do not cut a wide ad down and use it as a Short.
We do not promise people will watch longer. You can try another first few seconds, another actor, or another script, and you choose which file to publish.
Use [social media ad sizes](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform) before you download, and keep the product away from the buttons on the video player.

reviews.h2: How shops use YouTube Shorts ads
reviews.lead: A few ways shops open a Short from one product.

items.d: A kitchen shop uses a pan photo for one cook motion, with the handle kept visible.

items.t: A color swipe, then the tube
items.d: A beauty shop uses a gloss photo for a swipe of color, with the tube still visible.
An electronics shop uses an earbud case photo and shows the open case in a hand.
A drink seller uses a can photo for a short pour, with the label facing the camera.
A home shop uses a lamp photo for a switch-on, so the shade shape is easy to see.
A fitness shop uses a mat photo for an unroll, so the length is easy to see.
An apparel shop uses a jacket photo for one zip, with the collar kept visible.
A pet shop uses a brush photo for a short grooming pass so the size is easy to see.
A jewelry shop uses a necklace photo for a clasp close-up, with the chain fully visible.
An outdoor shop uses a bottle photo for a sip, so the logo stays easy to read.
